title: Suffering and the Edifying Love of Silence: Kierkegaard on Inwardness, Faith, and Existential Becoming
content: This article investigates suffering in Søren Kierkegaard from a central question: how can suffering be understood without reducing it to a psychological, medical, or explanatory object? The article argues that, in Kierkegaard’s thought, suffering can be understood as an existential experience that places the individual before the task of becoming singular. The analysis uses a philosophical-hermeneutic reading of selected works, especially *Either/Or*, *Fear and Trembling*, *Repetition*, *Works of Love*, and *Edifying Discourses in Various Spirits*. The argument articulates suffering, inwardness, silence, and indirect communication, examining the transition from ancient to modern tragedy, Antigone, Abraham as the paradigmatic figure of the Knight of Faith, and the edifying dimension of love. The analysis indicates that Kierkegaard’s treatment of suffering places the individual before the task of appropriating existence. Silence is not mere absence of speech, but a limit of direct communication in the face of singular experience. Indirect communication can preserve freedom by refusing to replace existential decision with a ready-made explanation. Finally, love does not abolish suffering; it can assume an edifying function by accompanying the sufferer without objectifying the experience.
